1: When I say “older women,” I mean women between about twenty and thirty: Women in their thirties were considered unmarriageable, because they were thought to be insufficiently fertile. And with this increasingly organized and ossified patriarchal social order, we see both a proliferation in the number of Monstrous Bitches and a diminution in their power.
2: Indeed, the Roman Monstrous Bitch is even further humanized than the Greek Monstrous Bitches from the last chapter. We’re not dealing with demons or demigods, nor with sorceresses who can conjure dragons, nor monsters whose bodies are half reptilian. We’re dealing, instead, with human women, who just happen to be able to bend nature and other human beings to their will through spellcraft.
3: As will surprise no one who’s made it to this point in this book, the origin for Canidia’s name is the Latin word for “dog,” so Canidia is literally a monstrous “bitch.” This Monstrous Bitch poses a real problem for Horace, not only because she unleashes chaos wherever she goes but also because Horace is obsessed with her.
4: Horace may vary the traits he assigns to Canidia in each of his works, but taken in the aggregate, they point toward his wanting to reanimate and recode the cultural DNA of Lamia and Medea for ancient Rome.
5: The message of the opening of The Aeneid, then, is that women are disposable, while men are essential to founding and protecting a new fatherland. Later, traveling with his son and followers in order to found Rome, Aeneas meets Queen Dido of Carthage, who is the most splendid literary ancient ruler I am aware of.
6: Does that sound like an outtake from The Bacchae crossed with The Eumenides? It should, because Virgil knows the same thing Euripides and Aeschylus know: Patriarchy cannot function if women raise their voices up together and take up arms against it. So, in the person of Amata, we have another critically important and entirely human Monstrous Bitch: She is a human female version of Dionysus.
7: So just as Tiamat was thrown down to form the ground we stand on, and just as the Furies were banished from Athens to the underrealms, Alecto eventually must find her way under the earth. Roman Patriarchy will now establish itself in blood and violence, with the threat of loudmouthed Bacchanalian matriarchy dispatched to the underworld, made abject once again. But not forever.
8: But what Lucan seems to find most terrifying about Erichtho is a trait she has that none of those other Monstrous Bitch incarnations have. She does not fear the gods. The Bacchae may not care about human patriarchs, or even about Zeus, but they sure do follow Dionysus.
9: Instead, much more like Medea, they’ve managed to weave themselves into the daily lives of regular people, where they will use their three core catastrophic powers entirely for their own benefit: slaying children and babies to eat their flesh and drink their blood, seducing and corrupting young men, and spellcasting to do all manner of nefarious magic. Reproductive harm, sexual harm, spellcasting harm.
10: Older woman enslaves man with vagina. Just to make very plain what is already explicit: The witches in this story are what we might today call cougars—older versions of Lamashtu, Lamia, Lilith, and Lilitu. They are seductresses of formidable sexual power, notwithstanding their age.
11: By the end of the second century CE, then, when Apuleius is writing, “lamia” had come to denote a Monstrous Bitch who was sexually predatory, baby-slaying, spellcasting, and violent. Now that Lamia has become lamiae, the threat of the Monstrous Bitch is potentially everywhere; she is an everywoman now, a witch who seduces men, casts her spells, and attacks the blood and bodies of children and young men.
12: Obyzouth and Gello aren’t human, and they’re not comic relief. They are deadly and deadly serious demonesses, sexy, seductive, baby-slaying, and woman-torturing. The classical Monstrous Bitch paradigm is thus very much intact in the Greek eastern Mediterranean, from the first century CE through the Middle Ages.
13: Like Lamashtu, Lilith casts herself as the semidivine progenitrix of infanticide. Like Tiamat, and like Lamashtu in her later iconography, Lilith has an army of followers and helpers; for Lamashtu/Lilitu, it’s the lilitus; for Lilith, it’s the liliths. Lilith and her army of liliths invade people’s homes, seducing husbands, strangling babies, and sucking out the blood of children.
14: Their main function, in all the regions in which they appear, is to cause reproductive havoc. They enjoy preying on babies and women not only to create this havoc but also for food: The äl eat their prey’s livers, lungs, and hearts. But they also destroy fetuses in the womb, prompting miscarriages.
15: So Romanitas didn’t tame and humanize Lamia everywhere. Where the full-fledged trope of Lamia undergoes truly massive change is in western Europe, where the twin patriarchates of Western Christianity and Roman culture flowed together.
